title: Seals and Sea Lions
objective: After this level you can tell seals from sea lions.
summary: Seals and sea lions are both pinnipeds. Sea lions have ear flaps, walk on their flippers and bark; seals have ear holes, wriggle on their bellies and are built for the water.

cards.headline: That "seal" balancing a ball at the aquarium show? Probably a sea lion.
cards.body: NOAA notes that sea lions are the ones more likely to star in marine shows. The two get mixed up all the time. A few quick clues and you never will again.

cards.headline: Flipper-footed
cards.body: Seals and sea lions belong to a group called pinnipeds, which means fin- or flipper-footed. Walruses are the third member. All of them are mammals that live in the ocean but can come on land for long stretches. They have a foot in each world, and each foot is a flipper.

cards.headline: Seal or sea lion? Check four clues

items.label: Seal
points: Wriggles on its belly on land

cards.headline: Built for different worlds
cards.body: Why the difference? Seals are better adapted to life in the water than on land, and they are more streamlined swimmers than sea lions. Their rear flippers can't rotate forward, so on a beach they hump along like caterpillars. Sea lions trade some of that sleekness for agility on land. A seal on a beach isn't clumsy; it's just off duty.

mascot.line: Quick test: flaps and a bark? Sea lion. Holes and a wriggle? Seal. You're officially dangerous at aquariums.

cards.headline: Seals vs. sea lions: sorted
learned: Pinnipeds: flipper-footed mammals of the sea
Sea lions: ear flaps, walk, paddle with front flippers, bark
Seals: ear holes, belly crawl, rear-flipper swimmers, quiet
Seals are the better swimmers; sea lions the better walkers

questions.prompt: Which clue tells you you're looking at a sea lion rather than a seal?

options.label: Small flaps on the outside of its ears
It wriggles along the beach on its belly
It swims by sweeping its rear flippers
It makes only soft grunts and hisses
options.rationale: Seals are the quiet ones; sea lions bark.

questions.explanation: Sea lions have small external ear flaps (they're called eared seals); true seals have only ear holes.

questions.prompt: A pinniped humps across the beach on its belly. Why can't it walk like a sea lion?

options.label: Its front flippers are too long
options.rationale: Long front flippers belong to sea lions.

options.label: It is a young sea lion that hasn't learned yet
options.rationale: Sea lions of all ages can walk.

options.label: Its rear flippers can't rotate under its body
It has ear flaps that throw off its balance
options.rationale: Ear flaps belong to sea lions and don't affect walking.

questions.explanation: Seals can't rotate their rear flippers forward, so on land they move on their bellies; sea lions rotate theirs to walk.

questions.prompt: Seals, sea lions and walruses are all pinnipeds. What links them?

options.label: They are fish that can breathe air
They live only on polar ice
options.rationale: They live in the ocean and come ashore in many places.

options.label: They all have external ear flaps
options.rationale: Only sea lions have ear flaps.

options.label: Flipper-footed mammals of the sea that come ashore

questions.explanation: Pinniped means fin- or flipper-footed: marine mammals that live in the ocean but can come on land for long periods.
